#Text=Milk is commonly preserved as condensed milk, and in this condition
#Text=is very valuable.
#Text=A pure condensed milk is now supplied, prepared
#Text=without the addition of sugar or any antiseptic, but in which, as in
#Text=other condensed milks, all disease-producing or decomposition-producing
#Text=microbes have been destroyed during the process of concentration.
#Text=Milk
#Text=may also be desiccated; in this condition it is difficult of digestion.
#Text=In addition to the household methods of preserving fruits, large
#Text=quantities of fruits—both moist and dry—are now imported, protected
#Text=by syrup or sugar, in sealed canisters; and they retain the original
#Text=flavour almost unchanged.
#Text=_Coffee._
#Text=
#Text=Coffee is a most powerful antiseptic, and therefore very useful as a
#Text=disinfectant.
#Text=It has been used as a specific against cholera with
#Text=marvellous results, and is useful in all cases of intestinal
#Text=derangement.
#Text=But only the pale-roasted varieties should be taken, as the
#Text=roasting develops the poisonous, irritating properties.
#Text=There is
#Text=_always_ danger in the roasting of grains or berries on account of the
#Text=new substances that may be developed.
#Text=_Grape._
#Text=
#Text=Sufferers from malaria may use grapes with great benefit.
#Text=For this
#Text=purpose the grapes, with the skins and stones, should be well pounded in
#Text=a mortar and allowed to stand for three hours.
#Text=The juice should then be
#Text=strained off and taken.
#Text=Or persons with good teeth may eat the grapes,
#Text=including the skins and stones, if they thoroughly macerate the latter.
#Text=_Onion Juice._
#Text=
#Text=The following prescription is excellent for sufferers from bronchitis or
#Text=coughs: Slice a Spanish onion; lay the slices in a basin and sprinkle
#Text=well with pure cane sugar.
#Text=Cover the basin tightly and leave for twelve
#Text=hours.
#Text=After this time the basin should contain a quantity of juice.
#Text=Give a teaspoonful every now and then until relief is afforded.
#Text=If too
#Text=much be taken it may induce headache and vomiting.
#Text=Poor fruit will not be improved by canning; over-ripe fruit will be
#Text=insipid and mushy; and though cooking will soften hard fruit, it cannot
#Text=impart to it the delicate flavors which belong to that which is in its
#Text=prime.
#Text=The larger varieties of fruit should not be quite soft enough for
#Text=eating.
#Text=Choose a dry day for gathering, and put up at once, handling as
#Text=little as possible.
#Text=Try to keep it clean enough to avoid washing.
#Text=If the
#Text=fruit is to be pared, use a silver knife for the purpose, as steel is
#Text=apt to discolor the fruit.
#Text=If the fruit is one needing to be divided or
#Text=stoned, it will be less likely to become broken if divided before
#Text=paring.
#Text==To Boil Cider.=
#Text=
#Text=Take cider which has been made but a day or two, and boil it nearly
#Text=half away.
#Text=Skim it often.
#Text=It will keep good a long time, and is useful
#Text=in making mince pies, and to flavor pudding sauce.
#Text=Bottle it and cork
#Text=it well.
#Text=A mould will form over the top, but will not injure the cider.
